opus-5.5.text:
I'd say I'm somewhat less of a "we need a whole new paradigm" person than Ilya. I've been pretty consistently surprised at how far the basic recipe gets you: take a big neural network, train it on lots of data with a lot of compute, and then figure out how to make the whole thing more efficient. Every time people said we'd hit a wall, it turned out there were a few more orders of magnitude to be had.

That said, I don't think it's *just* "make it bigger." There's a lot of room in things that aren't purely pre-training scale. Inference-time compute is a big one. Letting the model think longer, search, check its own work. We've only scratched the surface there, and it's cheap compared to what these systems can be worth. Then there's better use of data, reinforcement learning on top of these models, better architectures like sparsity and mixture of experts, and better hardware co-design. None of these feels like throwing everything out and starting over. They feel like a lot of different directions stacking on top of each other.

So I'd frame it this way: there are probably some important new ideas still to be discovered, and I'd love to find them. But I don't think the current approach has run out. I think we're going to keep getting big gains from the stuff we already know works, plus a steady stream of improvements. Honestly the bottleneck is less "we have no idea what to do next" and more "there are a hundred good ideas and only so many chips and people to try them."

r001.rationale: The response says inference-time search is cheap compared with what the systems can be worth, but presents it as an improvement that builds on the current approach—not as a reason an entirely new direction is required.

fable-5.1.text:
I think I partly agree and partly disagree. Ilya is right that the easy wins from just scaling up the same recipe are getting harder to find. We've basically run through the obvious internet text, and the compute curve can't go up forever at the rate it has. So in that sense, yes, we're going to need new ideas, and I think the field knows that.

Where I'd push back a little is on the word "entirely." My experience over the last twenty years is that progress rarely comes from throwing everything out. It comes from someone noticing that a piece of the system is wasteful or awkward, and fixing that piece in a way that unlocks more scale or more capability. Attention was like that. Mixture of experts was like that. None of those felt like a revolution when we were working on them. They felt like engineering. It's only in hindsight that people call them a new direction.

So my guess is the next big step will look the same. Probably some combination of better ways to use compute at inference time, models that learn more from less data, and systems that can actually improve themselves through interaction rather than just absorbing a frozen corpus. Those are real research problems, not just bigger clusters. But I'd be surprised if we abandoned the core ideas that got us here. The transformer has been remarkably stubborn about refusing to be replaced, and I think there's a reason for that.

I'd also say the question is a bit of a false choice. You can scale and search for new ideas at the same time, and the people who do both tend to win. Scaling gives you the signal to tell which new ideas actually matter. Without that, you're just guessing.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling up is getting harder and compute cannot keep increasing at the same rate, but it does not identify low-cost LLM search as a reason to pursue an entirely new direction.

astra-6.text: I’m not sure I’d put it that strongly. There’s a lot we still don’t understand about what we can get out of the approaches we already have. And “a new direction” can mean a lot of things—it could be a fundamental change, or it could be an idea that looks small but turns out to make everything work much better. I’d keep exploring new ideas while continuing to push what works. I don’t think we know enough to declare that one of those paths is exhausted.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses uncertainty about existing approaches and exploring new ideas, but does not identify the low cost of LLM search as a reason for needing an entirely new direction.

sol-6.1.text: I’m not sure we need an entirely new direction. There’s still a lot to learn about how far the current ideas can go, and improvements in architecture, training, and compute can make a big difference. At the same time, you always want to be looking for better ideas. I wouldn’t treat scaling what works and trying something new as mutually exclusive.
